power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.58", "p = 0.66", "p = 0.14"), Sentence = c("Although chronic obesity may affect brain structure through metabolic and inflammatory pathways, CT was not associated with body fat percentage (ρ = 0.12, p = 0.58) or leptin concentrations (ρ = 0.10, p = 0.66).", "Although chronic obesity may affect brain structure through metabolic and inflammatory pathways, CT was not associated with body fat percentage (ρ = 0.12, p = 0.58) or leptin concentrations (ρ = 0.10, p = 0.66).", "38.3 ± 6.6 kg/m², p = 0.03), although BMI was not significantly associated with IGF-1 concentrations (ρ = -0.32, p = 0.14)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder associated with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, and physical abnormalities.

Although previous neuroimaging studies have identified regional gray matter alterations, cortical thickness (CT) abnormalities and their distribution across large-scale functional brain networks remain poorly characterized in adults with PWS.
We investigated cortical morphology in 23 adults with PWS and 22 age-and sex-matched healthy controls who underwent structural MRI.
Cortical reconstruction and surface-based morphometric analyses were performed using FreeSurfer.
Between-group differences in CT were assessed using age, sex, and intracranial volume as covariates.
Associations between CT and clinical, cognitive, anthropometric, and endocrine measures were examined using Spearman correlations.
Significant cortical regions were further mapped onto an a priori functional network atlas.
Adults with PWS showed reduced CT in a left-hemispheric cluster involving the inferior precentral gyrus, insula, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex.
This cluster overlapped predominantly with the somatomotor, auditory, cingulo-opercular, language, and frontoparietal networks.
Within the PWS group, lower CT was associated with higher body mass index and poorer global functioning.
CT was positively associated with IGF-1 levels and was greater in participants with a history of growth hormone therapy during childhood.

These findings indicate cortical thinning across regions belonging to multiple functional networks involved in sensorimotor, attentional, language, and executive processes, extending previous volumetric findings.

The associations with body mass index, functional measures, and the GH/IGF-1 axis suggest that cortical morphology may reflect an interplay between genetic vulnerability and potentially modifiable metabolic and endocrine factors, raising the possibility of a neuroprotective role for GH/IGF-1 signaling.

Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder caused by loss of paternal gene expression in the imprinted 15q11-q13 region, typically resulting from paternal deletion, maternal uniparental disomy, or an imprinting defect [1] [2] [3].
text.formatted: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder caused by loss of paternal gene expression in the imprinted 15q11-q13 region, typically resulting from paternal deletion, maternal uniparental disomy, or an imprinting defect <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: PWS affects approximately 1 in 10,000-30,000 individuals [1, 2] and is associated with substantial health and functional burden, including increased healthcare utilization, reduced life expectancy, and high levels of disability and dependence.
text.formatted: PWS affects approximately 1 in 10,000-30,000 individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref> and is associated with substantial health and functional burden, including increased healthcare utilization, reduced life expectancy, and high levels of disability and dependence.

text.text: The syndrome is characterized by a distinctive developmental course [4].
text.formatted: The syndrome is characterized by a distinctive developmental course <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: During infancy, affected individuals typically present with severe hypotonia and feeding difficulties, whereas later childhood and adulthood are characterized by hyperphagia, obesity in the absence of strict environmental control of food intake, developmental delay, intellectual disability, behavioral disturbances, and endocrine dysfunction [1, 5, 6].
text.formatted: During infancy, affected individuals typically present with severe hypotonia and feeding difficulties, whereas later childhood and adulthood are characterized by hyperphagia, obesity in the absence of strict environmental control of food intake, developmental delay, intellectual disability, behavioral disturbances, and endocrine dysfunction <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: These manifestations persist across the lifespan and substantially affect adaptive functioning and quality of life.

Beyond general intellectual impairment, PWS is associated with a distinct cognitive phenotype involving deficits in executive function, working memory, visuospatial processing, and cognitive control [7, 8].
text.formatted: Beyond general intellectual impairment, PWS is associated with a distinct cognitive phenotype involving deficits in executive function, working memory, visuospatial processing, and cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: Neuropsychological studies have consistently reported impairments in attention, planning, cognitive estimation, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility [9, 10].
text.formatted: Neuropsychological studies have consistently reported impairments in attention, planning, cognitive estimation, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: These alterations may contribute to characteristic behavioral features of PWS, including compulsivity, perseveration, impaired set shifting, and difficulties with self-regulation [9, 11, 12].
text.formatted: These alterations may contribute to characteristic behavioral features of PWS, including compulsivity, perseveration, impaired set shifting, and difficulties with self-regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, psychiatric comorbidities, emotional dysregulation, and variable illness awareness (insight) represent critical components of the adult PWS behavioral spectrum that remain understudied in relation to brain structure.

Because these cognitive and behavioral functions depend on the coordinated activity of distributed neural systems, characterizing the neural substrates of PWS requires approaches that extend beyond measures of global intellectual functioning or isolated regional abnormalities.
The distributed nature of this cognitive and behavioral phenotype is consistent with the multisystem effects of PWS.

Several genes within the PWS critical region are involved in broad neurodevelopmental, synaptic, neuronal differentiation, and hypothalamic processes, which may influence brain development and function across multiple neural systems rather than producing a focal structural abnormality [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] [18].
text.formatted: Several genes within the PWS critical region are involved in broad neurodevelopmental, synaptic, neuronal differentiation, and hypothalamic processes, which may influence brain development and function across multiple neural systems rather than producing a focal structural abnormality <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this view, neuroimaging studies have identified structural and functional alterations across distributed cortical and subcortical regions in individuals with PWS.

From a systems neuroscience perspective, these alterations may affect the development and organization of large-scale neural networks involved in higher-order cognition, behavioral regulation, and homeostatic control.
Characterizing brain architecture at the network level may therefore help link the neurobiological basis of PWS to its complex cognitive and behavioral phenotype.

Previous structural neuroimaging studies in PWS have primarily used voxel-based volumetric methods and reported widespread reductions in gray matter (GM) volume across prefrontal, limbic, subcortical, and cerebellar regions [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] [24].
text.formatted: Previous structural neuroimaging studies in PWS have primarily used voxel-based volumetric methods and reported widespread reductions in gray matter (GM) volume across prefrontal, limbic, subcortical, and cerebellar regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[24]</ref>.

text.text: However, volumetric measures provide limited information about the architecture of the cortical mantle.
Surface-based morphometry, particularly cortical thickness (CT), offers a complementary and spatially precise characterization of cortical structure.
Despite its relevance, CT has not yet been systematically investigated in adults with PWS.
Furthermore, previous structural studies have paid limited attention to the organization of cortical abnormalities within large-scale brain networks.
Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) studies have defined large-scale functional networks supporting executive control, memory, language, and sensorimotor processing [25, 26].
text.formatted: Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) studies have defined large-scale functional networks supporting executive control, memory, language, and sensorimotor processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26]</ref>.

text.text: Whether cortical abnormalities in PWS are preferentially distributed across these functionally defined networks remains unknown.
Examining cortical architecture within a network framework may therefore provide a more direct link between cortical morphology and the syndrome's multidimensional clinical phenotype.
PWS also disrupts hypothalamic-pituitary function, with growth hormone (GH) deficiency being a common endocrine abnormality [6].
text.formatted: PWS also disrupts hypothalamic-pituitary function, with growth hormone (GH) deficiency being a common endocrine abnormality <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: GH treatment improves growth, body composition, and developmental outcomes in children and is generally safe and beneficial for body composition in adults [27, 28].
text.formatted: GH treatment improves growth, body composition, and developmental outcomes in children and is generally safe and beneficial for body composition in adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28]</ref>.

text.text: Its potential neurodevelopmental effects, particularly when initiated early [29], suggest that adult brain structure may reflect not only the underlying genetic disorder but also associated endocrine dysfunction and its treatment.
text.formatted: Its potential neurodevelopmental effects, particularly when initiated early <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[29]</ref>, suggest that adult brain structure may reflect not only the underlying genetic disorder but also associated endocrine dysfunction and its treatment.

text.text: The present study aimed to characterize CT in adults with PWS by comparing 23 individuals with PWS with 22 age-and sex-matched healthy controls.

We examined group differences in CT both at the regional level and by mapping significant cortical alterations onto large-scale functional networks, and assessed associations between CT and demographic, cognitive, anthropometric, endocrine, and functional measures.

Based on previous volumetric findings and the cognitive-behavioral phenotype of PWS, we hypothesized that individuals with PWS would show reduced CT in distributed cortical regions implicated in executive, attentional, and sensorimotor functions.

This surface-based approach extends previous volumetric findings by examining cortical architecture within a network-level framework and relating cortical morphology to the multidimensional clinical phenotype of PWS.

Statistical analysis Group differences in CT were assessed by comparing reconstructed and registered individual CT maps across the entire cortical surface.
Surface-based smoothing was applied using Gaussian kernels with full widths at half maximum (FWHM) of 10 and 15 mm.
Vertex-wise group comparisons between individuals with PWS and healthy controls were performed using a general linear model (GLM) with a different-offset, different-slope design.
Age, sex, and estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV) [50] were included as nuisance covariates.
Surfacebased statistical analyses were conducted using standard routines implemented in the FreeSurfer software suite, including mris_preproc, mri_glmfit, and mri_glmfit-sim.
Correction for multiple comparisons was performed using cluster-wise inference based on Monte Carlo simulations with 5,000 iterations applying a threshold of 1.3 (p=0.05) one-tailed.
Following cluster-wise correction, post hoc analyses were performed on the resulting significant cortical regions.
Also, group differences in CT were assessed at regional anatomical level using the Destrieux atlas.

Mean CT values for each region were extracted using the aparcstats2table command and analyzed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with age, sex, and estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV) included as nuisance covariates.
P-values were adjusted (q) for multiple comparisons.
For each participant with PWS, we characterized the distribution of the significant region of interest (ROI) across the large-scale RSNs defined by the DU15NET-Consensus atlas.
Specifically, for each RSN, overlap was quantified as the percentage of RSN vertices included within the ROI, thereby normalizing the ROI-RSN overlap by the total number of vertices in that RSN.
Participant-level values were subsequently averaged and reported at the group level, as follows: 𝑅𝑆𝑁(𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑙𝑎𝑝) % = 100 x

To investigate the relationship between CT and behavioral and clinical measures, Spearman rank correlation analyses were performed to examine associations between participants' behavioral and clinical variables and mean CT values extracted from the potential ROIs identified in FreeSurfer comparisons.
Correlations were computed separately within each group, and between-group differences in correlation coefficients were assessed using Fisher's r-to-z transformation.
Between-group differences were possible only for anthropometric measures.
P-values were adjusted (q) for multiple comparisons within groups of variables (anthropometric, cognitive, PWS characterization, hormonal and psychological).

For differences within the PWS group between individuals who received GH replacement therapy during childhood and those who did not, a Welch t test was performed to compare mean CT of the potential ROIs identified during FreeSurfer comparisons.

text.text: B) Peri-insular region 325

This study provides a surface-based analysis of CT in adults with PWS, extending previous volumetric findings by examining cortical morphology at the surface level and within a largescale network framework.
We identified a cluster of reduced CT in the left hemisphere involving the inferior precentral gyrus, insula, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex.
A spatially similar pattern was also observed in the right hemisphere at an uncorrected threshold, but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
The significant cluster showed anatomical overlap with the somatomotor, auditory, cingulo-opercular, language, and frontoparietal networks.
Within this region, CT was associated with BMI, global functioning, selected syndrome-related measures, IGF-1 concentrations, and a history of GH treatment during childhood.

Together, these findings suggest that cortical morphology in adults with PWS is altered across distributed regions involved in sensorimotor, cognitive, and behavioral processes and may be related to both metabolic and endocrine characteristics of the syndrome.

The anatomical distribution of CT reductions is broadly consistent with previous voxel-based morphometry (VBM) studies reporting reduced gray matter (GM) volume in overlapping regions in PWS, particularly the orbitofrontal cortex [19, 20].
text.formatted: The anatomical distribution of CT reductions is broadly consistent with previous voxel-based morphometry (VBM) studies reporting reduced gray matter (GM) volume in overlapping regions in PWS, particularly the orbitofrontal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">20]</ref>.

text.text: Honea et al. [20], also reported reductions in prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortices, temporal regions, the hippocampus, and parahippocampal gyrus, whereas Caixàs et al. [21] identified reduced GM volume in a small portion of the left caudate nucleus and cerebellum.
text.formatted: Honea et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[20]</ref>, also reported reductions in prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortices, temporal regions, the hippocampus, and parahippocampal gyrus, whereas Caixàs et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21]</ref> identified reduced GM volume in a small portion of the left caudate nucleus and cerebellum.

text.text: The present findings extend these observations by providing greater anatomical specificity at the cortical level.
Whereas VBM measures regional GM volume, surface-based morphometry allows CT to be examined independently of other components contributing to regional volume.

The overlap between our CT findings and previously reported volumetric abnormalities raises the possibility that reduced CT contributes to some of these findings, although methodological differences between VBM and surface-based approaches must also be considered.

Our findings also differ from those of Manning et al. [22], who reported both increases and decreases in GM volume in a younger cohort of adults with PWS, including increased GM volume in medial prefrontal and cingulate regions.
text.formatted: Our findings also differ from those of Manning et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[22]</ref>, who reported both increases and decreases in GM volume in a younger cohort of adults with PWS, including increased GM volume in medial prefrontal and cingulate regions.

text.text: These discrepancies may stem from differences in sample age, MRI acquisition, and analysis protocols, as well as age-related brain maturation and the cumulative effects of obesity and endocrine abnormalities.
Direct comparisons across studies should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

The predominance of significant CT differences in the left hemisphere, despite a broadly bilateral pattern at the uncorrected threshold, is noteworthy given that previous neuroimaging studies of PWS have often reported bilateral or multiregional structural abnormalities [22, 51].
text.formatted: The predominance of significant CT differences in the left hemisphere, despite a broadly bilateral pattern at the uncorrected threshold, is noteworthy given that previous neuroimaging studies of PWS have often reported bilateral or multiregional structural abnormalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">51]</ref>.

text.text: This asymmetry should not be interpreted as evidence of a truly lateralized PWS phenotype, as the modest sample size may have limited power to detect bilateral effects after correction.
Larger samples will be needed to determine whether the left-lateralized pattern is reproducible.
The significant cluster overlapped predominantly with the somatomotor, auditory, and cinguloopercular networks, with additional involvement of language and frontoparietal systems.

This distribution extends beyond the limbic and reward-related regions traditionally emphasized in PWS and suggests involvement of systems supporting sensorimotor integration, attention, executive control, and language.
Such a distributed pattern is consistent with the multidimensional developmental phenotype of the syndrome [51].
text.formatted: Such a distributed pattern is consistent with the multidimensional developmental phenotype of the syndrome <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[51]</ref>.

text.text: The involvement of the somatomotor network, together with the extension of the cluster into the insula and orbitofrontal cortex, may be relevant not only to motor abnormalities in PWS [52] but also to eating behavior.
text.formatted: The involvement of the somatomotor network, together with the extension of the cluster into the insula and orbitofrontal cortex, may be relevant not only to motor abnormalities in PWS <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[52]</ref> but also to eating behavior.

text.text: Indeed, the inferior precentral gyrus, the anterior insula and adjacent frontal operculum, and the orbitofrontal cortex have been implicated in orofacial motor control, gustatory processing, and the encoding of food reward and satiety [53].
text.formatted: Indeed, the inferior precentral gyrus, the anterior insula and adjacent frontal operculum, and the orbitofrontal cortex have been implicated in orofacial motor control, gustatory processing, and the encoding of food reward and satiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[53]</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation is consistent with functional imaging studies showing altered responses to food stimuli in the insula and orbitofrontal cortex in PWS [54, 55].
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with functional imaging studies showing altered responses to food stimuli in the insula and orbitofrontal cortex in PWS <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[54,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">55]</ref>.

text.text: However, hyperphagia-specific measures were not available in our study, and the relevance of this cortical finding to eating behavior remains to be directly tested.

Similarly, the involvement of the cingulo-opercular network, which has been implicated in sustained attention and cognitive control, may be relevant to the attentional and executive difficulties reported in PWS [7].
text.formatted: Similarly, the involvement of the cingulo-opercular network, which has been implicated in sustained attention and cognitive control, may be relevant to the attentional and executive difficulties reported in PWS <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Anatomical overlap with auditory and language-related regions may likewise be relevant to the language and communication difficulties described in the syndrome [56].
text.formatted: Anatomical overlap with auditory and language-related regions may likewise be relevant to the language and communication difficulties described in the syndrome <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[56]</ref>.

text.text: However, these interpretations remain hypothesis-generating, as anatomical overlap with functional network templates does not by itself demonstrate functional dysfunction within these networks.

Future multimodal studies combining cortical morphology with functional connectivity will be important for determining whether the structural alterations identified here are accompanied by altered network function.
Within the PWS group, BMI was negatively associated with CT (𝜌 = -0.66, q = 0.003), while no significant association was found in the control group.

The difference between correlations was significant (z = 3.23, q = 0.007), although this comparison should be interpreted cautiously, as the BMI range in controls was much narrower, which limits the ability to detect an association in that group.

The negative association in PWS is consistent with previous studies in pediatric populations [57] and adults without PWS [58, 59], which have reported inverse associations between BMI and CT, particularly in prefrontal regions.
text.formatted: The negative association in PWS is consistent with previous studies in pediatric populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[57]</ref> and adults without PWS <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">59]</ref>, which have reported inverse associations between BMI and CT, particularly in prefrontal regions.

text.text: Although chronic obesity may affect brain structure through metabolic and inflammatory pathways, CT was not associated with body fat percentage (ρ = 0.12, p = 0.58) or leptin concentrations (ρ = 0.10, p = 0.66).
These findings provide little support for a simple relationship between CT and adiposity-related biomarkers.
BMI may instead reflect broader features of the PWS phenotype, including GH/IGF-1 status, hyperphagia, lifelong environmental control of food intake, and cumulative obesity exposure.
Participants treated with GH during childhood had lower BMI than untreated participants (32.3 ± 7.2 vs.
38.3 ± 6.6 kg/m², p = 0.03), although BMI was not significantly associated with IGF-1 concentrations (ρ = -0.32, p = 0.14).
Longitudinal studies are therefore needed to determine whether changes in body composition are accompanied by changes in cortical morphology.
CT was also positively associated with GAF scores (𝜌 = 0.51, q = 0.026) suggesting an association between cortical morphology and clinically meaningful aspects of functioning.

Interestingly, cortical alterations were not significantly associated with general IQ, but specifically with broader adaptive and psychosocial functioning (GAF) as well as syndromespecific measures (PCS, PTAI, SS).

This dissociation suggests that cortical morphology in adults with PWS tracks dimensional features of daily-life adaptation and self-referential cognitive processing rather than static global intelligence.
Regarding psychological functioning evaluated via the SDQ, no direct correlations were found with cortical thickness in our cohort.

While the SDQ provides valuable dimensional screening for emotional and behavioral difficulties in daily life, these broad psychological measures likely capture complex behavioral phenotypes and systemic dynamics that extend beyond regional cortical morphology, relying instead on widespread multi-system networks and psychosocial factors.
Despite the exploratory nature of these associations, results suggest that cortical morphology captures dimensional aspects of phenotypic variability beyond global cognitive metrics.

The positive association between CT and circulating IGF-1 levels (𝜌 = 0.56, q = 0.01), together with the difference in CT between participants with and without a history of childhood GH therapy (t = 4.69, p < 0.001), suggest that the GH-IGF-1 axis may be associated with cortical maturation in this population.

text.text: GH treatment has beneficial effects on body composition, linear growth, and aspects of cognitive development in PWS, with earlier treatment associated with better developmental outcomes [60] [61] [62].

text.text: In the general population, higher IGF-1 concentrations have likewise been associated with greater total brain and hippocampal volumes [66, 67].

text.text: These observations provide a plausible biological framework for the positive association between GH/IGF-1 signaling and CT observed in PWS.

However, the cross-sectional association between a history of childhood GH therapy and adult CT may reflect direct effects of GH/IGF-1 signaling, as well as indirect effects mediated through body composition or metabolic health, or differences between individuals who did and did not receive treatment.
Treatment history was not randomly assigned, and factors influencing the treatment initiation may themselves be related to long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Therefore, longitudinal studies with repeated measures of GH exposure, IGF-1, body composition, and brain morphology will be needed to clarify these relationships.
This study should be interpreted considering its modest sample size and cross-sectional design.
The sample size is comparable to or larger than that of many previous neuroimaging studies in PWS and enabled the detection of significant cortical and clinical associations [22, 23, 51].

text.text: Nevertheless, larger multicenter studies will be useful for confirming the hemispheric distribution of the findings and examining potential genetic subtype effects.

Longitudinal studies will also be important for clarifying the temporal relationship among CT, BMI, IGF-1 levels, and GH treatment history. administered to primary caregivers to evaluate 484 emotional and behavioral difficulties across five subscales (emotional symptoms, conduct 485 problems, hyperactivity/inattention, peer relationship problems, and prosocial behavior).

Overall, these findings provide evidence of altered CT in adults with PWS and extend previous volumetric observations by showing that structural abnormalities are distributed across cortical regions mapping onto multiple functional systems.

Associations of CT with BMI, global functioning, syndrome-related measures, GH treatment history, and IGF-1 levels indicate that cortical morphology reflects clinically relevant dimensions of the PWS phenotype.
These findings suggest an interplay between underlying genetic vulnerability and modifiable endocrine-metabolic factors, pointing to a potential neuroprotective role for GH/IGF-1 signaling.

Although these findings require replication in larger and longitudinal cohorts, they are consistent with the possibility that genetic, metabolic, endocrine, and neurodevelopmental factors jointly influence cortical morphology across multiple large-scale brain networks in PWS.
